questions_and_answers.question_text: Which object precedes the other — the indirect or the direct?
What is the word order of a blunt imperative in Chinese?
How do you make a polite request in Chinese?
What does qǐng mean more literally?
Write the Chinese for "Please give me two catties."
What is the idiomatic equivalent of qǐng and qǐng ni?
How does the Chinese word order of a blunt imperative compare with English?

answers.answer_text: It is the same: (Nǐ), verb, indirect object, direct object.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "Give me two catties." as a blunt imperative.
What does the verb gěi mean?
Name the three types of imperative given in the note.

answers.answer_text: The blunt imperative (Gěi wo liǎngjīn), the polite request with qǐng (Qǐng gěi wo liǎngjīn), and the polite request with qǐng ni (Qǐng ni gěi wo liǎngjīn).

articles.text:
3. A: Gěi wo liǎngjīn.                     Give me two catties.

4. A: Qǐng ni gěi wo liǎngjīn.             Please give me two catties.

Notes on Nos. 3-4

Indirect object: Notice that the indirect object, wo, precedes the direct object, liǎngjīn, just as "me" precedes "two catties" in English.

Gěi  |  wo  |  liǎngjīn.
(Give | me  |  two catties.)

Polite requests: A blunt imperative in Chinese has the same word order as a command in English: (Nǐ), verb, indirect object, direct object. To make a polite request in Chinese, start off with qǐng, "please," or qǐng ni, "please you." More literally, qǐng means "to ask," "to request," but the idiomatic equivalent of qǐng and qǐng ni is "please." Here are the three types of imperatives:

Gěi         |     |  wo  |  liǎngjīn.     (Give me two catties.)
Qǐng        |     |  gěi wo  |  liǎngjīn. (Please give me two catties.)
Qǐng  | ni  |  gěi  |  wo  |  liǎngjīn.   (Please give me two catties. OR
                                          Give me two catties, please.)
